¶
'''warm-heartedness''' (wârm′här″ted-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being warm-hearted; affectionate disposition; cordiality.
{{smaller block|He was looking from Arabella to Winkle with as much delight depicted in his countenance as ''warm-heartedness'' and kindly feeling can communicate to the human face.
{{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick.}}}}

'''warming''' (wâr′ming), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''warm'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of one who warms; specifically, in silver-plating, the heating of the object to be plated until it causes a slight hissing when immersed in water. {{smaller|The object is then dipped in dilute nitric acid, to cause a slight roughening of the surface in order to afford a better hold to the silvering.}} '''2.''' A castigation; a thrashing. [Colloq.]

'''warming-pan''' (wâr′ming-pan), ''n.'' '''1.''' A large covered long-handled flat vessel (usually of brass) into which live coals are put: used to warm the inside of a bed.
{{smaller block|Put of your clothes in winter by the fire side, and cause your bed to bee heated with a ''warming panne.''
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 252.}}
A dagger with a hilt like a ''warming-pan.''
{{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, iv. 4. 33.}}}}
'''2.''' A person put into a situation, post, or office temporarily, to hold it for another till the latter becomes qualified for it. [Slang.]

{{RunningHeader|warm|6825|warn}}'''2.''' Heated; having the sensation of heat; exhibiting the effects of being heated to a moderate degree; hence, flushed. {{smaller block|’Twas well, indeed, when ''warm'' with wine, To pledge them with a kindly tear. {{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xc.}}}} '''3.''' Communicating a sensation of warmth, or a moderate degree of heat: as, a ''warm'' fire; ''warm'' weather.—'''4.''' Subject to or characterized by the prevalence of a comparatively high temperature, or of moderate heat: as, a ''warm'' climate; ''warm'' countries.—'''5.''' Intimate; close; fast: as, ''warm'' friends.—'''6.''' Hearty; earnest: as, a ''warm'' welcome; ''warm'' thanks. {{smaller block|The conduct of Hampden in the affair of the ship-money met with the ''warm'' approbation of every respectable Royalist in England. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}}} '''7.''' Fresh: said of a scent or trail.—'''8.''' Close to something that is sought, as in games involving search or guessing; on the right track; on the way to success, as in searching or hunting for something. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|He ’s ''warm''—he ’s getting cold—he ’s getting colder and colder—he ’s freezing. {{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, iii. 6.}}}} '''9.''' Comfortable; well-off; moderately rich; in easy circumstances. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|''Water-Camlet.'' Believe it, I am a poor commoner.
''Sir F. Cres.'' Come, you are ''warm'', and blest with a fair wife. {{right|''Middleton'', Anything for a Quiet Life, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|We have been thinking of marrying her to one of your tenants, . . . a ''warm'' man, . . . able to give her good bread. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xvi.}}}} '''10.''' Comfortably fixed or placed; at home; acquainted; well adjusted. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|A gentleman newly ''warm'' in his land, sir. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Scarcely had the worthy Mynheer Beekman got ''warm'' in the seat of authority on the South River than enemies began to spring up all around him. {{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 409.}}}} '''11.''' Undesirable; unpleasant, as on account of unpopularity or obnoxiousness to law, etc. {{smaller block|Their small Stock of Credit gone, Lest Rome should grow too ''warm'', from thence they run. {{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Eleventh Satire of Juvenal.}}}} '''12.''' Ardent; earnest; full of zeal, ardor, or affection; enthusiastic; zealous. {{smaller block|I’me half in a mind to transcribe it, and let it go abroad in the Catalogue; but I’me sensible the ''warm'' people of two opposite parties will be ready to blame my forwardness. ''Humphrey Wanley'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 288).}} {{smaller block|When she saw any of the company very ''warm'' in a wrong opinion, she was more inclined to confirm them in it than oppose them. {{right|''Swift'', Death of Stella.}}}} {{smaller block|Now ''warm'' in love, now with’ring in my bloom, Lost in a convent’s solitary gloom! {{right|''Pope'', Eloisa to Abelard, l. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|Till a ''warm'' preacher found a way t’ impart Awakening feelings to his torpid heart. {{right|''Crabbe'', Works, V. 74.}}}} '''13.''' Animated; brisk; keen; heated; hot: as, a ''warm'' engagement. {{smaller block|We shall have ''warm'' work on ’t. {{right|''Dryden'', Spanish Friar, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|He argued with perfect temper in society, or, if he saw the argument becoming long or ''warm'', in a moment he dashed over his opponent’s trenches, and was laughingly attacking him on some fresh point. {{right|''Lady Holland'', Sydney Smith, vii.}}}} '''14.''' Stirred up; somewhat excited; hot; nettled: as, to become ''warm'' when contradicted. {{smaller block|A fine boggle-de-botch I have made of it. . . . I am aware it is not a canonical word — classical, I mean; nor in nor out of any dictionary perhaps — but when people are ''warm'' they cannot stand picking terms. {{right|''Miss Edgeworth'', Helen, xxvi.}}}} '''15.''' Having the ardor of affection or passion. {{smaller block|Mirth and youth and ''warm'' desire. {{right|''Milton'', May Morning.}}}} {{smaller block|The enactments of human laws are vain to restrain the ''warm'' tides of the heart. {{right|''Sumner'', Orations, I. 239.}}}} '''16.''' Having too much ardor; coarse; indelicate. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|I do not know the play; but, as Maria says, if there is any thing a little too ''warm'' (and it is so with most of them) it can be easily left out. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Mansfield Park, xv.}}}} '''Warm bath''', in ''med.'', a bath in water of a temperature from 92° to 98° F.—'''Warm colors''', in ''painting'', such colors as have yellow or red for their basis: opposed to ''cold colors'', as blue and its compounds: the term, however, is a relative one.—'''Warm plaster.''' See ''plaster''.—'''Warm register''', a heated register-plate used in the manufacture of tarred ropes.—'''Warm sepia.''' See ''sepia''.—'''Warm wave.''' See ''wave''1.—'''Warm with''', an abbreviation for “warm with sugar,” as in the order given for a beverage of that sort, in contrast with ''cold without''. [Slang.] {{smaller block|Two glasses of rum-and-water ''warm with''. {{right|''Dickens'', Sketches.}}}} ='''Syn. 4.''' Sunny, mild, close, oppressive.—'''6.''' Earnest, hearty, enthusiastic, eager.—'''1-6.''' ''Warm'' is distinctly weaker than ''hot'', ''fervent'', ''fervid'', ''fiery'', ''vehement'', ''passionate''. '''II.''' ''n.'' '''1†.''' Warmth; heat. {{smaller block|The winter’s hurt recovers with the ''warm''; The parched green restored is with shade. {{right|''Surrey.''}}}} '''2.''' An act or process of warming; a heating. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|Boil it [barley-malt] in a kettle; one or two ''warms'' is enough. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 151.}}}} '''warm''' (wârm), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''warmed'', ppr. ''warming''.   [< ME. ''warmen'', < AS. ''wearmian'' (= D. ''warmen'' = MHG. ''warmen'', G. ''wärmen'' = Icel. ''verma'' = Dan. ''varme'' = Sw. ''värma'' = Goth. ''warmjan''), become warm, < ''wearm'', warm: see ''warm'', ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To become warm or moderately heated; communicate warmth. {{smaller block|Wyndis wastid away, ''warmyt'' the ayre; The rede beames aboue blusshet with hete. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4036.}}}} {{smaller block|All are but parts of one stupendous whole, . . . That, changed through all, and yet in all the same, . . . ''Warms'' in the sun, refreshes in the breeze. {{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 271.}}}} '''2.''' To warm one’s self. {{smaller block|There shall not be a coal to ''warm'' at. {{right|Isa. xlvii. 14.}}}} '''3.''' To become ardent, animated, or enthusiastic. {{smaller block|I know the full value of the snood; and MacCallummore’s heart will be as cold as death can make it when it does not ''warm'' to the tartan. {{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xxxv.}}}} {{smaller block|As the minister ''warms'' to his sermon there come through these cracks frequent exclamations. {{right|''W. M. Baker'', New Timothy, p. 73.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' To make warm. {{smaller|(''a'') To communicate a moderate degree of heat to; impart warmth to.}} {{smaller block|And there, withoute the dore, in ye courte on the left hand, is a tree with many stones aboute it, where the mynysters of the Jewes, and seynt Peter with theym, ''warmed'' theym by the fyre. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|Either the hostess or one of her maids ''warms'' his bed, pulls on his night cap, cuts his corns, puts out the candle. {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, v. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The room is ''warmed'', when necessary, by burning charcoal in a chafingdish. {{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, I. 20.}}}} (''b'') To heat up; excite ardor or zeal in; interest; animate; enliven; inspirit; give life and color to; flush; cause to glow. {{smaller block|It would ''warm'' his spirits To hear from me you had left Antony. {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 13. 69.}}}} {{smaller block|With those hopes Socrates ''warmed'' his doubtful spirits against that cold potion. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Urn-burial, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|I love such mirth as does not make friends ashamed to look upon one another next morning, nor men that cannot well bear it to repent the money they spend when they be ''warmed'' with drink. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 87.}}}} {{smaller block|How could I, to the dearest theme That ever ''warm’d'' a minstrel’s dream, So foul, so false a recreant prove! {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|All beauty ''warms'' the heart, is a sign of health, prosperity, and the favor of God. {{right|''Emerson'', Success.}}}} (''c'') To administer castigation to: as, I’ll ''warm'' him for that piece of mischief. [Colloq.] (''d''†) Figuratively, to occupy. {{smaller block|His brother . . . had a while ''warmed'' the Throne. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 84.}}}} '''To warm one’s jacket''', to castigate one. [Colloq.]—'''Warming plaster.''' See ''plaster''. '''war-man''' (wâr′man), ''n.'' A warrior. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Thir lordis keipt on at afternoone, With all thair ''warrmen'' wight. {{right|''Battle of Balrinnes'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 222).}}}} {{smaller block|The sweet ''war-man'' is dead and rotten. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 666.}}}} '''war-marked†''' (wâr′märkt), ''a.'' Bearing the marks or traces of war; experienced in war; veteran. {{smaller block|Your army, which doth most consist Of ''war-mark’d'' footmen. {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 7. 45.}}}} '''warm-blooded''' (wârm′blud″ed), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having warm blood; hematothermal: in zoölogy and physiology noting mammals and birds whose blood ranges in temperature from 98° to 112° F., in consequence of the complete double blood-circulation, and the oxygenation or combustion which goes on in the lungs: opposed to ''cold-blooded'' or ''hematocryal.''—'''2.''' Figuratively, characterized by high temper and generous impulses; warm-hearted; also, passionate.—{{smaller|'''Warm-blooded fish.''' See ''fish''1.}} '''warmer''' (wâr′mėr), ''n.''   [< ''warm'' + ''-er''1.]   One who or that which warms. '''warmful†''' (wârm′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''warm'' + ''-ful.'']   Giving warmth; warm. [Rare.] {{smaller block|About him a mandilion, that did with buttons meet, Of purple, large, and full of folds, curl’d with a ''warmful'' nap. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, x. 121.}}}} '''warm-headed''' (wârm′hed″ed), ''a.'' Easily excited; enthusiastic; fanciful. {{smaller block|The advantage will be on the ''warm-headed'' man’s side, as having the more ideas and the more lively. {{right|''Locke.''}}}} '''warm-hearted''' (wârm′här″ted), ''a.'' Having warmth of heart; having a disposition such as readily shows friendship, affection, or interest; proceeding from such a disposition; cordial; sincere; hearty: as, a ''warm-hearted'' man; ''warm-hearted'' support. '''warm-heartedness''' (wârm′här″ted-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being warm-hearted; affectionate disposition; cordiality. {{smaller block|He was looking from Arabella to Winkle with as much delight depicted in his countenance as ''warm-heartedness'' and kindly feeling can communicate to the human face. {{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick.}}}} '''warming''' (wâr′ming), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''warm'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of one who warms; specifically, in silver-plating, the heating of the object to be plated until it causes a slight hissing when immersed in water. {{smaller|The object is then dipped in dilute nitric acid, to cause a slight roughening of the surface in order to afford a better hold to the silvering.}} '''2.''' A castigation; a thrashing. [Colloq.] '''warming-pan''' (wâr′ming-pan), ''n.'' '''1.''' A large covered long-handled flat vessel (usually of brass) into which live coals are put: used to warm the inside of a bed. {{smaller block|Put of your clothes in winter by the fire side, and cause your bed to bee heated with a ''warming panne.'' {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 252.}}}} {{smaller block|A dagger with a hilt like a ''warming-pan.'' {{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, iv. 4. 33.}}}} '''2.''' A person put into a situation, post, or office temporarily, to hold it for another till the latter becomes qualified for it. [Slang.] '''warming-stone''' (wâr′ming-stōn), ''n.'' A foot-warmer; a slab of soapstone, cut to a convenient size: when used it is first heated in the fire or on a stove, and afterward placed under the feet: it is chiefly made use of in driving in very cold weather. {{smaller|Soapstone is selected for this purpose because it stands the heat better than any other stone, not cracking or crumbling when exposed to sudden changes of temperature.}} '''warmly''' (wârm′li), ''adv.'' In a warm manner. {{smaller|(''a'') With warmth or heat.   ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 244. (''b'') With warmth of feeling; eagerly; earnestly; ardently.}} {{smaller block|Each prince shall thus with honour have What both so ''warmly'' seem to crave. {{right|''Prior'', Alma, ii. 111.}}}} '''warmness''' (wârm′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''warmness''; < ''warm'' + ''-ness''.]   Warmth. {{smaller block|Phebus hath of gold his stremes doun ysent To gladen every flour with his ''warmness''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 977.}}}} '''war-monger†''' (wâr′mung″gėr), ''n.'' One who fights for hire; a mercenary soldier, or bravo.   ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. x. 29. '''warmouth''' (wâr′mouth), ''n.'' A centrarchoid fish: same as ''bigmouth''. '''warm-sided''' (wârm′sī″ded), ''a.''   ''Naut.'', mounting heavy guns: said of a ship or a fort. [Colloq.] '''warmth''' (wârmth), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wermthe'' (= LG. ''wermde''); < ''warm'' + ''-th''1.]   '''1.''' The state of being warm; gentle heat: as, the ''warmth'' of the sun or of the blood; also, the sensation of moderate heat. {{smaller block|No ''warmth'', no breath, shall testify thou livest. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 1. 98.}}}} {{smaller block|The mirth of its December, And the ''warmth'' of its July. {{right|''Praed'', I remember, I remember.}}}} '''2.''' Cordiality; geniality; hearty kindness or good feeling. {{smaller block|I took leave of Colonel Cubbon, who told me, with a ''warmth'' which I was vain enough to think sincere, that he had not passed three such pleasant days for thirty years. {{right|''Macaulay'', in Trevelyan, I. 325.}}}} '''3.''' A state of lively and excited feeling; ardor; zeal; fervor; earnestness, often approaching anger; intensity; enthusiasm. {{smaller block|What ''warmth'' is there in your affection towards any of these princely suitors? {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 2. 36.}}}} {{smaller block|The sisters fell into a little ''warmth'' and contradiction. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 172.}}}} {{smaller block|The monarch spoke; the words, with ''warmth'' addrest, To rigid justice steel’d his brother’s breast. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, vi. 78.}}}} '''4.''' In ''painting'', a glowing effect which arises from the use of warm colors (which see, under ''warm''), and also from the use of transparent colors in the process of glazing. '''warn†''' (wârn), ''n.''   [< ME. ''warne'', < AS. ''wearn'', a denial, refusal, obstacle, impediment, a guarding of oneself, a defense of a person on trial, = OHG. ''warna'' (in comp.), MHG. ''warne'', ''werne'', preparation, = Icel. ''vörn'' = Sw. ''värn'' = Dan. ''værn'', a defense; with formative ''-n'', < Teut. √ ''war'', defend, guard: see ''ware''1, ''ward''.]   A denial; refusal. {{smaller block|Withouten more ''warne''. {{right|''Cursor Mundi'', l. 11333.}}}} '''warn''' (wârn), ''v. t.''   [Under this word are merged two orig. diff. but related verbs: (''a'') < ME. ''warnen'', ''warnien'', warn, admonish, < AS. ''wear-''
